facts.text: Off-road braking differs from road braking in magnitude and dominant influences, but not in the underlying physics.
facts.quote: Off-road braking differs from road braking in magnitude and in what dominates it, not in the physics.

facts.text: Mass cancels in a friction-limited point-mass stopping model.
facts.quote: In a friction-limited point-mass stop, mass cancels

facts.text: Stopping on earth-moving machines is affected by finite and thermally limited brake torque, payload-induced changes to center of gravity and axle or track loads, severe grades, deformable ground, and braking by the drivetrain itself.
facts.quote: brake torque is finite and thermally limited, payload moves the center of gravity and the axle or track loads, grades are severe, the ground deforms, and the drivetrain itself may brake

facts.text: New South Wales guidance specifies a 0.60 m/s² in-service minimum off-road deceleration.

facts.text: US MSHA Table M-1 specifies a constant deceleration of 9.66 ft/s², approximately 2.94 m/s².

facts.text: UN R152 specifies a braking demand of at least 5.0 m/s² for car automatic emergency braking.
facts.quote: a braking demand of at least 5.0 m/s² for car automatic emergency braking under UN R152

facts.text: Brake latency is a first-order contribution to stopping distance at work-site speeds.
facts.quote: Latency is a first-order term at work-site speeds.

facts.text: A published 2026 brake-response figure for a tracked-vehicle electro-hydraulic brake is under 0.3 s.
facts.quote: under 0.3 s for a tracked-vehicle electro-hydraulic brake (2026)

facts.text: A published 2025 brake-response figure for a mining electric vehicle's brake-by-wire is 0.41 s.

facts.text: A published 1989 brake-response figure for road air brakes is about 0.5 s.
facts.quote: about 0.5 s for road air brakes (1989)

facts.text: The MSHA regulation specifies system response times of 0.5 s to 2.5 s by weight class.

facts.text: Historic haul-truck work reported retarder lag of 1 s to 2 s.

facts.text: At speeds of 5 km/h to 15 km/h, latency can account for half or more of stopping distance.
facts.quote: At 5 km/h to 15 km/h the latency term can be half or more of the stopping distance.

facts.text: Modern delay distributions for production wheel loaders, articulated haulers and haul trucks were not found.
facts.quote: Modern delay distributions for production wheel loaders, articulated haulers and haul trucks were not found.

facts.text: Grade and payload change available deceleration by an amount of the same order as the deceleration itself.
facts.quote: Grade and payload shift available deceleration by the same order as the deceleration itself.

facts.text: Under the New South Wales formulas, a 100 t rigid truck designed for a 20% grade but tested on a 9% grade needs 1.79 m/s² deceleration on the test grade.
facts.quote: In the New South Wales formulas a 100 t rigid truck designed for a 20% grade but tested on 9% needs 1.79 m/s² on the test grade

facts.text: For the New South Wales formula example of a 100 t rigid truck designed for a 20% grade and tested on 9%, the grade correction alone is about 1.04 m/s².
facts.quote: the grade correction alone is about 1.04 m/s²

facts.text: A NIOSH stopping model found parameter combinations in which downhill grade exceeded brake capacity and the simulated machine did not stop.
facts.quote: A NIOSH stopping model found parameter combinations where a downhill grade exceeded brake capacity and the simulated machine did not stop

facts.text: A 2015 on-road simulation showed a grade-blind braking trigger that worked at 0% grade but resulted in collisions at 11% and 17% grades.
facts.quote: an on-road simulation (2015) showed a grade-blind trigger that worked at 0% grade and collided at 11% and 17%

facts.text: The recommended core stopping-distance model is a calibrated point-mass model with measured latency, a brake build-up lag, and worst-case deceleration dependent on grade, payload and surface.
facts.quote: A calibrated point-mass model with measured latency, a brake build-up lag and a worst-case deceleration that depends on grade, payload and surface is the right core model for stopping distance.

facts.text: Higher-fidelity stopping models pay off only for brake-actuation hydraulics and latency spread, articulated and high-center-of-gravity stability under hard braking, operating-state-dependent hydrostatic braking capacity, and soft or deformable ground.
facts.quote: Higher fidelity pays off in four places only: brake-actuation hydraulics (latency and its spread), articulated and high-center-of-gravity stability under hard braking, hydrostatic drives whose braking capacity varies with operating state, and soft or deformable ground.

facts.text: A 2026 on-road simulation round robin found that more complex vehicle models produced spreads of 0.033 s and 0.314 m, whereas point-mass models reproduced the prescribed profile exactly.
facts.quote: A 2026 simulation round robin showed that more complex vehicle models produced a 0.033 s and 0.314 m spread where point-mass models reproduced the prescribed profile exactly

facts.text: Greater vehicle-model complexity does not imply greater accuracy.
facts.quote: complexity is not accuracy
